In any case, find the real canonical form of A. That is find P ∈ M2×2(R) invertible such that P −1AP is of one of the following form(λ1 0 0 λ2 ), (λ 1 0 λ ) or ( a b −b a ) . Proof. pA(x) = det(xI − A) = det ( x − 1 −1 3 x − 1 ) = (x − 1) 2 + 3 = (x − 1 − √3i)(x − 1 + √3i). pA(x) does not splits in R, hence A is not diagonalizable over R. pA(x) splits in C with distinct linear factors, A is diagonalizable over C. To find the real canonical form, we consider an eigenvalue of A λ = 1 + √3i. We solve 0 = (λI − A)v = (√3i −1 3 √3i ) v = 0 to get v = c ( 1√ 3i ). Thus with P = (Re v, Im v) = (1 0 0 √3 ) we have P −1AP = ( 1 √3 − √3 1 ) . 2 Problem 3. Let A = 1 2 ( −1 −4 1 3 ) , and f (x) = log(1 − x) = −x − x2 2 − x3 3 − · · · = − ∞∑ k=1 xk k . Let A, B ∈ Mn×n(F ). If v is an eigenvector of AB with eigenvalue λ ̸= 0, show that Bv is an eigenvector of BA with eigenvalue λ. Proof. We have BA(Bv) = B((AB)v) = Bλv = λ(Bv). To show that Bv is an eigenvector, we show that Bv ̸= 0. We have A(Bv) = (AB)v = λv for λ ̸= 0. Since v is an eigenvector, we have v ̸= 0 and hence A(Bv) = λv ̸= 0. Thus Bv ̸= 0 (since otherwise A(Bv) = 0). 4 Problem 5. Suppose that A ∈ M2×2(R) is symmetric. Prove that A is diagonalizable over R. Proof. Since A is symmetric, we write A = ( a b b c ) for a, b, c ∈ R. Then pA(x) = det ( x − a −b −b x − c ) = (x − a)(x − c) − b2 = x2 − (a + c)x + ac − b2 = (x − λ1)(x − λ2) where with (a + c)2 − 4(ac − b2) = a2 − 2ac + c2 + 4b2 = (a − c)2 + 4b2 we have λ1 = a + c + √(a − c)2 + 4b2 2 , λ2 = a + c − √ (a − c)2 + 4b2 2 . If b = 0, then A = diag(a, c) is diagonalizable over R. If b ̸= 0, then (a − c)2 + 4b2 > 0 and λ1, λ2 are distinct real numbers. Then pA(x) splits as distint linear factors in R. Hence A is diagonalizable over R. 5 Problem 6. Let A ∈ Mn×n(R) satisfy A2 = −I. (i) Show that n = 2m is even and det(A) = ±1. (ii) Show that i and −i are both eigenvalues of A in C. (iii) Show that A is diagonalizable over C. (iv) Show that tr(A) = 0 and that dim E(i, A) = dim E(−i, A) = m. (v) Find the characteristic polynomial pA(x). (vi) Show that det(A) = 1. (vii) Find det(I − A). Proof. (i) (det(A))2 = det(A2) = det(−I) = (−1)n. Since A ∈ Mn×n(R) we have (−1)n = (det(A))2 > 0 and thus n = 2m is even. Since (det(A))2 = 1, we have det(A) = ±1. (ii) Let λ ∈ C be an eigenvalue of A. Then λ2 = −1. Thus λ = ±i. Since A ∈ Mn×n(R), if λ is an eigenvalue of A, so is ¯λ. Thus both i and −i are eigenvalues of A. (iii) Let f (x) = x2 + 1. Since f (A) = A2 + I = 0, we have mA(x) | f (x). Since f (x) = (x − i)(x + i) splits in C as distinct linear factors, so is mA(x). Thus A is diagonalizable over C. (iv) We set dim E(i, A) = k. Since A is diagonalizable, dim E(−i, A) = n − k and there is P ∈ Mn×n(C) invertible such that P −1AP = diag(i, . . . , i ︸ ︷︷ ︸ k times , −i, . . . , −i ︸ ︷︷ ︸ n−k times ). We have tr(A) = ki − (n − k)i = (n − 2k)i. Since A ∈ Mn×n(R), we have tr(A) ∈ R. Thus we must have n − 2k = 0 i.e. k = m. (v) pA(x) = (x − i)m(x + i)m = (x2 + 1)m. (vi) det(A) = (−1)n det(A) = pA(0) = 1. (vii) det(I − A) = pA(1) = 2m. 6
